abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: The growing demand for sustainable, high-performance energy storage systems has spurred intensive research into biomass-derived carbon materials as environmentally friendly electrode candidates for supercapacitors. In this study, Murraya koenigii (curry plant) seed powder was employed as a novel biomass precursor for the synthesis of activated carbon in the presence of ferrous chloride (FeCl2) as an activating agent (MKAC). The FeCl2-mediated activation, followed by pyrolysis at 900 °C under an inert atmosphere, facilitated the formation of a hierarchically porous carbon structure rich in electrochemically active sites. Comprehensive structural and chemical characterisation via BET analysis, FTIR, XRD, SEM-EDAX, and Raman spectroscopy confirmed the formation of partially graphitised carbon with an enhanced surface area of approximately 1605.5 m2 g− 1. Symmetric supercapacitor cells were assembled using a conductive polymer gel electrolyte based on poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVdF-HFP). Electrochemical evaluation demonstrated that FeCl2 activation synergistically contributed to low internal resistance and a superior specific capacitance of 221.3 F g− 1 at a current density of 0.5 mA cm− 2, with an energy density of 15.37 Wh kg− 1 at a power density of 217 W kg− 1. The fabricated symmetric EDLC device retains ~ 88% of its initial capacitance after 10,000 consecutive charge-discharge cycles with a Coulombic efficiency of ~ 88%, confirming the long-term electrochemical stability and charge reversibility of the MKAC electrode. This green and economically viable approach not only adds value to agricultural waste but also offers a viable pathway toward developing advanced electrode materials for sustainable supercapacitor applications.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The growing energy demand in the world and the dwindling fossil fuels have heightened the quest for sustainable and clean energy storage systems. Electrochemical supercapacitors have also become an option of interest among other alternatives because of their high-power density, fast charge-discharge rate, and extended cycle life, among other factors. They are intermediaries between traditional dielectric capacitors and rechargeable batteries1─3. The selection of electrode material and electrolyte system is the main factor that defines the overall performance of the supercapacitors1. Here, the emergence of inexpensive, renewable, and energy-dense electrode materials based on biomass feedstock has received considerable interest in recent years3.

The valorisation of agricultural and food waste into high-performance carbon electrode materials represents a strategically important and scalable pathway for sustainable energy storage. Recent advances have demonstrated that biomass-derived carbons encompassing plant residues, crop waste, and food by-products can be engineered through chemical and physical activation to yield hierarchically porous architectures with large surface areas, tunable pore distributions, and intrinsic heteroatom functionalities that collectively enhance both double-layer and pseudocapacitive charge storage. The translation of laboratory-scale biomass carbonisation processes to pilot and commercial scales is increasingly feasible, as the raw materials require no elaborate purification, the synthesis protocols are compatible with conventional industrial furnaces, and the activating agents such as FeCl2, ZnCl2, and KOH are commercially available at low cost. These attributes, combined with the zero-cost nature of agricultural residues and their year-round availability across agrarian economies such as India, collectively position biomass-derived carbon as a commercially compelling alternative to synthetic or mined electrode materials for next-generation energy storage devices.

The development of activated carbon made from biomass is of great importance. Due to its renewability, availability, and inherent heteroatom functionality, it has the potential to increase the electrochemical activity of electrochemical devices. In addition, the functional properties of activated carbon produced from biomass possess the electronic, porous, and chemically active surfaces required to optimize the electrode materials of electrochemical devices. The way activated carbon has been published can also be seen in the surface area, porosity, and surface chemistry properties that have been designed by different activation techniques, both physical and chemical, to create the porous structure necessary for high-performance electrochemical devices4. The physical method of activation, steam, carbon dioxide (CO₂) or air, will create the pores in the carbon structure through gas-phase etch. The resulting pores created by the physical activations are generally larger (meso- to macropores), and the surface area created by the activation is moderate (approximately 1300-1500m2 g− 1) in most cases of activated oil palm shell5. In contrast, chemical activation integrates carbonisation and activation into a single process at temperatures of approximately 450 to 850 °C, resulting in significantly higher surface areas and ultramicroporosity6. Chemical activating agents are substances such as acids (e.g., phosphoric or sulfuric acid), bases (e.g., potassium or sodium hydroxide), and metal salts (e.g., zinc chloride or iron (III) chloride) used to increase the porosity and surface area of carbonaceous materials6. In this process, the activating agent is typically impregnated into a carbon-rich precursor (such as wood or biomass) and then heated under an inert atmosphere to promote activation. Chemical activation by using transition metal salts has been identified as an effective strategy for causing hierarchical porosity and enhancing electrical conductivity7. Specifically, it has been found that ferrous chloride (FeCl2) can be used as a dual-functional agent, not only by catalytically graphitising during pyrolysis but also by etching carbon skeletons, and hence synthesising fully developed porous carbons with partially graphitic domains7, 8.

FeCl2-activated carbons are characterised by the fact that the iron salt not only produces a high BET surface area and a well-developed microporous structure but also adds iron and oxygen-containing surface groups that serve as redox-active sites, thereby enhancing pseudocapacitive contributions9. In comparison to the more traditional KOH activation, which results in the largest surface areas (often exceeding 2,000 m2 g− 1) and provides a specific capacitance of 244 F g− 1 in a 1 M H₂SO₄ electrolyte for molasses-derived carbon material10 derived from FeCl2 achieves similar or even higher capacitance in organic and ionic-liquid electrolytes (with reported values reaching approximately 334 F g− 1)11. Due to the synergistic effect of Fe-induced redox activity and enhanced wettability.

The zinc chloride (ZnCl2) activated carbon produced by this process has very good porosity and more acidic oxygenated groups than phosphoric acid (H3PO4) activated carbons. However, zinc chloride-activated carbons lack high specific capacitance because their surface areas are very low. Phosphoric acid-activated carbons have many mesoporous pores and a large number of phosphorus functional groups, which are useful for transporting ions between the carbon surface and the electrolyte, yet typically achieve specific capacitance values between 200 and 250 F g− 112, which are lower than the values produced by ferrous chloride (FeCl2) activated carbons. Therefore, carbon produced from FeCl2 activation is a combination of a very high surface area and redox-active iron sites, providing excellent specific capacitance properties, especially when used with non-aqueous electrolytes.

Murraya koenigii (L.) Spreng. commonly known as curry tree is a perennial aromatic shrub or small tree within the Rutaceae family, and widespread across most of the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. The leaves, seeds, bark and roots of this plant all have many quantities and types of bioactive and carbon-rich compounds and for those reasons hold great value from a plant biology point of view. The seeds of the Murraya koenigii plant are very unique compared to other seeds because they have a very tightly arranged structure made up primarily of organic matter, which contains a high percentage of the following types of lignocellulosic material (cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin) and phytochemical compounds (carbazole, alkaloids, flavonoids and phenolics) and several types of less abundant compounds that have heteroatoms13,─15.

A plethora of research supports the ability of Murraya koenigii as a potential renewable material source for carbonaceous functional materials. The leaves, stems, and seeds of Murraya koenigii have been extensively studied for their use as activated carbons and biochars for numerous purposes, including environmental remediation-based applications, biomedical uses, and energy-related applications, with mesoporous structures being particularly noteworthy due to their substantial anti-tumour, anti-inflammatory, and anti-diabetic effects, thus demonstrating good biocompatibility and active surfaces in16. Activated carbons obtained from stems and seeds have also been investigated as relatively inexpensive adsorbents to adsorb organic dyes, including methylene blue, Acid Red 18 and crystal violet from water, demonstrating good adsorption kinetics and surface affinity17 ─19. Our research group has also recently identified activated carbon materials created from Murraya koenigii seeds, also microporous in nature, as potential electrode materials for supercapacitors using ZnCl2 as an activation agent20, validating the potential of this biomass for electrochemical energy storage.

However, ZnCl₂ and FeCl₂ represent fundamentally different activation chemistries with distinct structural outcomes. ZnCl2 functions primarily as a Lewis acid catalyst, promoting dehydration reactions and selective pore formation, typically yielding mesopore-dominant structures. FeCl2, on the other hand, serves a dual role: it catalyses partial graphitisation through iron-carbide intermediate pathways during pyrolysis while simultaneously etching the carbon framework to generate a highly microporous architecture. Importantly, the residual iron species was confirmed by EDAX. The present study, therefore, represents a systematic investigation of how the choice of metal salt activating agent fundamentally governs pore architecture, surface chemistry, and electrochemical response of the same biomass precursor, a mechanistic comparison of significant scientific value.

The seeds of Murraya koenigii (often referred to as an underutilised biowaste material with natural heteroatomic, alkaloids and lignocellulosic biomass, and thus suitable as a precursor resource to sustainably develop electrode materials2, 20, 21. There are, however, very few reports concerning their valorisation on energy storage devices. This paper has used Murraya koenigii seed powder activated via FeCl2 and then carbonised to produce a porous carbon material, which has increased textural and electrochemical characteristics. The surface and structural properties were examined with different characterisation techniques, and the results proved the creation of a partially graphitised and porous carbon structure.

Polymer gel electrolytes have been characterised by high ionic conductivity, leakage-proof, non-corrosive, good interfacial contact with electrodes, and mechanical flexibility, thus can be used in practical supercapacitor applications22─25. The interaction between the FeCl2-activated carbon derived from Murraya koenigii seeds (MKAC) electrodes and the polymer gel electrolyte yields a superior electrochemical response because of the balance between the conductivity, ion transportation, and stability of the structure.

sec.title: Preparation of activated carbon electrode material
sec.p: The reagents of this study included ferrous chloride tetrahydrate (FeCl2.4H2O), ethanol, hydrochloric acid and acetone, which were acquired at Fisher Scientific, Avarice Chemicals and Qualigens, respectively. Murraya koenigii seeds were locally obtained from Mahendergarh, Haryana, in India. The first step was to prepare a sample from the seeds, which was done similarly in our previous work20. For the activation of the seeds, the powdered seeds were mixed with FeCl2 in a weight ratio of 1:2, and the mixture was mixed in a solvent, ethanol, to form a uniform slurry. To achieve full soaking and chemical interaction, this slurry was left to air dry at room temperature over a period of about 6 to 7 days. The pyrolysis was also maintained at ∼900 °C in the presence of nitrogen (N2) gas with a ramp rate of 5 °C min− 1 and a dwell time of 30 min. The inert environment played an imperative role in avoiding contamination by oxygen. The material was cooled to room temperature following the pyrolysis and ground into a fine powder. The rest of the inorganic was removed by washing in diluted HCl, and then the deionised water until a neutral pH was achieved. The dried material was then dried in a vacuum at ∼100 °C overnight, and kept in air-tight containers so as not to absorb moisture. A diagrammatic model of the whole preparation procedure is shown in Fig. 1.

sec.title: Fabrication of supercapacitor cell
sec.p: The FeCl2-activated carbon derived from Murraya koenigii seeds (MKAC) powders was used in the preparation of supercapacitor electrodes for device assembly. A homogenous slurry was prepared by mixing 95 wt% of selected active material and 5 wt% poly (vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVdF-HFP), a binder. This slurry was sprayed on flexible sheets of graphite, approximately 250 μm thick, which were the current collectors, and are resistant to corrosion and have mechanical strength. The electrodes were coated and dried overnight in a vacuum at ∼100 °C, and the active loading of the material was maintained at approximately 1 mg cm− 2. Murraya koenigii seed-derived activated carbon (MKAC) electrodes were used to construct symmetric supercapacitor cells with a 1 × 1 cm2 area. The polymer electrolyte membrane was prepared in the form of a liquid electrolyte mixture of ethylene carbonate (EC), propylene carbonate (PC) and sodium perchlorate (NaClO4) using PVdF-HFP host polymer by solution casting26. sec.p: To explore the structural, morphological, and electrochemical characteristics of activated carbon derived from Murraya koenigii seeds (MKAC), a thorough characterisation was conducted utilising a range of advanced analytical instruments. The surface area, pore size and pore structure parameters were assessed from N2 adsorption-desorption isotherms collected at 77 K, employing the BELSORP Data Analysis Software (BELMaster, Ver. 7.2.0.4, MicrotracBEL, Corp.). The crystallographic structure was investigated using two complementary X-ray diffractometers: an XtaLab Synergy Custom equipped with a RA-MicroMax 007HF Generator and a HyPix 6000 detector, and a PANalytical Empyrean multipurpose diffractometer. Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) using a PerkinElmer Spectrum within the wavenumber range of 4000–400 cm− 1. The structural ordering and degree of graphitisation were examined via Raman spectroscopy with a Renishaw inVia confocal micro-Raman spectroscope, using a 532 nm wavelength.

sec.title: Structural and morphological studies
sec.p: The Nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherm shows that the activated carbon derived from Murraya koenigii seeds (MKAC) material is a high-surface-area, micro-mesoporous carbon with an H4-type hysteresis loop and slit-like pores. At higher pressures, the slope shows increased uptake of adsorbate as pores become filled. The material has a very large BET area, with the majority of the total pore volume being made by micropores, as shown in Table 1. The adsorption-desorption isotherm exhibits steep uptake at extreme relative pressure P/Po less than 0.05, which is typical of micropore filling, then multi-layer adsorption, and a relatively small hysteresis loop over the mesopore region, which is typical of a mixed Type I(b) and IV(a) isotherm27, 24. The loop form is equivalent to the hysteresis of the type of material with slit-like pores and micro-mesopores structures that IUPAC correlates with the presence of sharp uptake and narrow loop shapes initially seen in Fig. 3 (a). The adsorption branch was used to determine the surface area of the BET, finding the linear region that meets the Rouquerol consistency criteria of positive C, monotonically increasing n (1-P/Po) with P/Po and a self-consistent monolayer capacity, usually within 0.05 ≤ P/Po ≤ 0.30 with N2 at 77 K according to IUPAC guidelines24, 25, 28─30.

(a) N2 adsorption-desorption isotherms, (b) Pore size distribution of activated carbon powders MKAC.

sec.p: The SBET of the MKAC in this validated range is ∼1605.5 m2 g− 1, indicating a large number of accessible surfaces formed by the activation and supportive of the micro-mesoporous isotherm form, which is way more than both the in Murraya koenigii seeds carbon (MKC), and ZnCl2-activated Murraya koenigii seeds20. The total pore volume (Vtotal) is 0.9444 cm3 g− 1, and the micropore volume (Vmicro) is 0.7154 cm3 g− 1, which means that the portion of the total pore volume occupied by the micropores in this specimen is ∼75.7%. The micropore surface area (Smicro) of t-plot analysis is 1346.4 m2g− 1, which is a confirmation that the vast bulk of the measured SBET is of micropores, whereas a smaller fraction of mesopores facilitates the diffusion pathways, which is typical of micro-mesoporous carbons. The result of the BJH analysis is the differential distribution of pore-area (Fig. 3(b)), which has a significant portion at approximately 2.3 nm with a rapidly decreasing tail towards small mesopores, in agreement with the H4 loop and the micro- mesoporous classification.

The X-ray diffraction (XRD) was used to investigate the crystallographic properties of Murraya koenigii seeds-derived activated carbon (MKAC), and the resulting diffractogram was analysed by X’Pert HighScore. The strongest diffraction peak was found at about ~ 24.3° (referring to the (002) plane), shown in Fig. 4(a), which is attributable to the typical turbostratic structure of disordered carbon, validating partial graphitic ordering31. Using the Bragg law, the interplanar spacing (d-spacing) has been determined. Where n is the order of reflection, is the wavelength at which the peak corresponds, θ is the half of the diffraction angle (2θ), and d is the interplanar spacing, which is found to be ∼3.66 Å.

sec.p: The value of d-spacing is in agreement with the previous reports of biomass-derived activated carbons20. Further, the crystallite size was also calculated by means of the Scherrer equation,

K is the shape factor, is the 1.5406 Å (Cu -Kα- radiation), β is the full width at half maximum (FWHM), and θ is the Bragg angle. Based on this estimate, crystallite size was determined to lie between ~ 3 nm of nanoscale sizes of ordered carbon layers in the predominantly amorphous matrix. The defective and porous structure with large defects and broadened peak profile is confirmed by the small crystallite size and extended profile of the peak. The experimental XRD peaks demonstrate a strong correlation with the standard diffraction patterns found in the ICDD Powder Diffraction File (PDF) database, specifically matching PDF entries 96–210-1125 and 96–231-0615, as determined through the use of X’Pert HighScore Plus software. These sources relate to graphitic-like carbon phases, which are disordered stacked, which also confirms that there exists the presence of graphitic domains within the amorphous carbon matrix. The XRD pattern is a sharp, weaker reflection at 2θ around ~ 35° as seen in Fig. 4(a). This peak is unusual for pure carbon, but it could also show the existence of an iron-containing residue in the carbon structure. Since FeCl2 has been used for activation of Murraya koenigii seeds, it is reasonable that after acid wash, some of our iron species survived to become iron oxides (e.g., magnetite, Fe3O4 or maghemite) or iron-carbide (Fe3C) phases during pyrolysis. Indeed, it is known that magnetite generates a strong (311) reflection at approximately ~ 35° in XRD analyses of FeO4/carbon composites32 and the EDAX data confirm the remains of Fe. This type of structural arrangement has the advantage of facilitating the use of supercapacitors in that the combination of amorphous and partially graphitised carbon facilitates ion movement, accessibility, and conductivity of the surface.

Further Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was used in order to determine the remaining functional groups on the surface of the activated carbon derived from Murraya koenigii seeds (MKAC). Several sharp absorption peaks at 3757, 3630, 2981, 2897, 2326, 2095, 1547 and 1152.8 cm− 1 are observed in the FTIR spectrum of the MKAC (Fig. 5). The pyrolysis, especially at high temperature ∼900 °C, is aimed to decomposing the complex organic compounds of the original biomass, and all volatile compounds. The fact that there are only a few functional groups left on the pyrolysed carbon surface directly corresponds to a very weak signal of absorption in the infrared spectrum31.

caption.p: FT-IR pattern for Murraya koenigii seeds derived activated carbon (MKAC).

sec.p: The wide bands at ∼3630 and ∼3757 cm− 1 are attributed to O-H vibrations. The rather sharp peak at around 3757 cm− 1 represents non-hydrogen bonded hydroxyl groups, the peak at around 3630 cm− 1 represents hydrogen-bonded hydroxyls or phenolic O-H. Their existence shows that the phenolic and hydroxyl functionalities which are formed by the natural phenols and flavonoids of Murraya koenigii, remain intact even after chemical activation and high-temperature carbonisation, contributing to the surface polarity of the activated carbon. The C-H region has two bands, around 2981 and 2897 cm− 1, which are said to be aliphatic C-H stretching (-CH2/-CH3). Such bands are a reflection of the leftover aliphatic fragments of the biomass31, 33, 34. The band at ∼2325.55 cm− 1 is typically found in porous carbonaceous materials and is attributed to the asymmetric stretching vibration of adsorbed or atmospheric CO2, which is commonly detected in FTIR spectra35. The peak at ∼2095 cm− 1 could be a definite cumulative bond character (conjugated C = C), which could be obtained through the condensed aromatic derivatives in the starting material35. The peak at ∼1547 cm− 1 is likely to be a result of the aromatic ring vibrations34. The occurrence of this band indicates the structure of the material to be composed of a highly condensed and polyaromatic structure of carbon.

After that the structure and the degree of graphitisation of the activated carbon derived from Murraya koenigii seeds (MKAC) were studied using Raman spectroscopy. Figure 4(b) displays the deconvoluted Raman spectrum in the wavelengths of 200–2500 cm− 1 and the two distinct bands are the D band at ∼1353 cm− 1 and the G band at ∼1590 cm− 1, which is typical of carbonaceous materials. The D band at ~ 1353 cm− 1 is a result of the A1g breathing mode of six-membered carbon rings, and can only occur in the presence of disorder. The G band around ~ 1590 cm− 1 can be attributed to E2g stretching of sp2 bond, observed in both the ordered and disordered carbons. An elevated ID/IG ratio indicates more chaos and defects in the carbon framework, and the increase in disorder-defect density increased number of sp2 ring-breathing defect mode also linked to greater microporosity, heteroatom integration and edge location, capable of improving capacitance through wettability36. Estimation of the level of defect in carbons is generally done using the ID/IG ratio. As the ID/IG ratio exceeds unity, the material is regarded as highly disordered and has a lower degree of graphitic ordering. This may be attributed to the processes of activation of the material by introducing heteroatoms, oxygenated groups or edges. A Similar trend has been reported for FeCl2-activated carbon derived from Murraya koenigii seeds (MKAC), where the ID/IG ratio increased to ∼2.26, compared to 0.82 for the non-activated carbon (MKC)20, which signifies the presence of more defects and lower graphitic order in activated carbon derived from Murraya koenigii seeds (MKAC)32, 37. Interestingly, the expansion of the D band also validates that there are also many structural defects and functional groups that are oxygenated, which are beneficial in electrochemical processes38─43. In brief, the Raman examination shows that the activation of the biowaste precursor using FeCl2 has able to achieve a balanced microstructure of both ordered graphitic and defect-rich amorphous carbon.

The surface morphology and elemental compositions of the Murraya koenigii seeds-based activated carbon via FeCl2 (MKAC) and Murraya koenigii seeds-based non-activated carbon (MKC) were analysed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDAX) as depicted in Fig. 6. The SEM micrograph in Fig. 6(a) of MKC indicates a rather dense and compact appearance with low porosity, indicating that the pore has not developed fully throughout the pyrolysis process. Conversely, in Fig. 6(b), the MKAC is more open, irregular, and fragmented in its morphology, with the pore formation and roughness of the surface being clearly visible, also evident by BET. It is the process of soaking in FeCl2 and pyrolysing at ∼900 °C in 3 h that seems to allow the enhancement of catalytic gasification and rearrangement of structure, surface texturing and the generation of other electroactive sites42, 44─46.

caption.p: SEM images and EDAX graph and data of (a) Murraya koenigii seeds derived non-activated carbon (MKC) (b) Murraya koenigii seeds derived activated carbon (MKAC).

sec.p: The success of the activation of carbon with FeCl2 is also supported by the EDAX spectra and the compositional data (Fig. 6). Carbon is still the primary component in the Murraya koenigii seeds-derived activated carbon (MKAC) (82.12 wt%), although the amount of oxygen in the sample (10.81 wt%) is significantly higher in the MKAC than it is in the MKC (7.85 wt%). The greater concentration of oxygen implies that it does contain oxygen-containing surface functionalities, which are known from FTIR. Furthermore, the presence of iron (6.0 wt%) and chlorine (0.6 wt%) in the Murraya koenigii seeds-derived activated carbon (MKAC) indicates the existence of the leftover species of FeCl2 treatment even after acid washing. Those traces of metals can serve as the redox-active centres, which can additionally increase charge storage capacity. In general, the SEM-EDAX analysis shows that the activation of FeCl2 changes the morphology of the carbon by creating the surface porosity, which was also witnessed in BET47.

sec.title: Electrochemical studies
sec.p: Electrochemical studies were performed by three techniques which where electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), cyclic voltammetry (CV) and galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD) as discussed below.

Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was used to analyse the charge transport properties and the capacitive behaviour, along with the resistive behaviour of the prepared electrodes of MKAC in electrochemical devices. The Nyquist, Bode and phase angle plot, and the equivalent circuit fit can be seen in Fig. 8 (a-d) in the frequency range of 100 kHz to 10 mHz. Figure 8(a) indicates that in the high-frequency region of the Nyquist plot, the small value at the real axis corresponds to the series resistance (Rs) of the electrolyte and the electrode-electrolyte interfaces. It was found that the value of Rs across has been about ~ 7.7 Ω cm− 2, indicating that the proper contact at the electrode-electrolyte interface, and polymer gel electrolyte provides sufficient ions48. At medium frequencies, a semicircle occurs, which is indicative of the charge transfer resistance (Rct) associated with ion exchange within the electrodes at the interface. The value of Rct of the cell has been determined to be approximately 6.7 Ω cm− 2, significantly less than that of the MKC electrode-based supercapacitor cell, which has been discussed in detail in our previous study20, confirming the increased conductivity and kinetics of charge transfer provided by FeCl2-assisted activation47,49,50. The capacitive behaviour predominates, which can be observed via a near vertical line of the Nyquist plot in the low frequency region51, 52. The given feature permits the well-developed hierarchical porosity to be created in the course of activation, making it feasible to carry ions fast and increase capacitive performance up to ∼190.7 F g− 1 (Table 2).

sec.p: The impedance spectra were analysed using a modified Randles equivalent circuit obtained from Zview2 software, which includes a series resistance (Rs), two combinations of parallel resistance and constant phase elements ((R₁‖QPE₁) and (R₂‖CPE₂)), followed by a Warburg diffusion element (Ws)53, as depicted in Fig. 7, and values are mentioned in the fitting parameter Table 3. The series resistance is almost matched with respect to the experimentally observed values mentioned above in Table 2. The relatively low value of Rs indicates effective interfacial contact and efficient ionic conduction through the PVdF-HFP-based gel electrolyte. The first parallel branch, defined by R₁ and CPE₁, is associated with the rapid interfacial charge transfer process and the non-ideal formation of the double-layer at the porous carbon surface. The high n value 0.88, which is close to unity, suggests a primarily capacitive response with minimal surface heterogeneity. EDLCs utilising porous carbon electrodes (AC, MWCNTs, SWCNTs, GNP) indicate that the value of n is reported to range from 0.6 to 0.854. The second parallel branch, consisting of R₂ and CPE₂, relates to deeper ion penetration and distributed capacitance within the hierarchical pore network of the activated carbon, indicating increased surface roughness and variability in pore size53. The finite-length Warburg short element (Ws) was selected in the equivalent circuit model in preference to the open Warburg element (Wo), based on the physical diffusion behaviour of the present system. The open Warburg element (Wo) is physically appropriate only when ion diffusion occurs across a semi-infinite, unbounded diffusion layer, a condition typically applicable to planar, open electrode surfaces in bulk liquid electrolytes. In contrast, the MKAC electrode possesses a well-defined hierarchical microporous architecture with finite pore lengths, within which electrolytic ion diffusion is geometrically constrained and bounded by the pore walls. Under these conditions, ions cannot diffuse to infinite depth, and the diffusion layer thickness is limited by the physical dimensions of the micropores. The Warburg short element (Ws) accurately models this bounded, finite-length diffusion behaviour, where ion transport occurs within the microporous channels. This physical justification is consistent with the predominantly microporous character of the MKAC electrode confirmed by BET analysis (69.5% microporosity)55, 56.

caption.p: Fitting parameters of Impedance spectra using Zview2 software for MKAC electrodes.

sec.p: The Bode plot of the MKAC-based symmetric EDLC device, presenting the frequency dependence of the total impedance magnitude log|Z| (left Y-axis) and the phase angle (right Y-axis) over the frequency range of 10− 2 Hz to 105 Hz, is illustrated in Fig. 8 (b). At high frequencies, the impedance magnitude attains a minimum plateau value, reflecting the dominance of the equivalent series resistance (Rs) of the system, while the phase angle approaches 0° characteristic of purely resistive behaviour at elevated frequencies. With progressive decrease in frequency, log|Z| increases monotonically, indicative of the capacitive charge storage becoming increasingly dominant at lower frequencies. Correspondingly, the phase angle shifts systematically toward more negative values, reaching approximately − 74° to −76° at the lowest measured frequency (10− 2 Hz), the deviation from the ideal − 90° is attributed to the distributed capacitance within the microporous architecture and minor ion diffusion limitations within the narrow pore channels of the MKAC electrode. The characteristic response frequency (fo), defined as the frequency at which the resistive and capacitive impedances are equal and identified at a phase angle of −45°, was determined to be 0.1468 Hz from the Bode phase plot. From this, the relaxation time constant (τ₀) was calculated as 6.81 s. This relaxation time constant represents the minimum time required to discharge more than 50% of the stored energy from the device with high efficiency, and the relatively low τ₀ value obtained confirms the rapid charge-discharge kinetics and good frequency response of the MKAC-based symmetric supercapacitor, attributable to the well-developed hierarchical microporous network facilitating efficient electrolytic ion transport within the PVdF-HFP gel electrolyte matrix47, 51, 57─61. Figure 8(c) illustrates the frequency dependence of the imaginary component of capacitance (Cʺ) for the EDLC. A distinct maximum in Cʺ is noted in the low-frequency range, which corresponds to the characteristic relaxation process of the electrode-electrolyte system. This peak signifies the transition from resistive behaviour at high frequencies to capacitive charge storage at low frequencies, where electrolyte ions have adequate time to reach the porous carbon surface and establish a stable electric double layer62. The movement of the Cʺ maximum towards lower frequencies suggests a relatively short relaxation time constant, indicating effective ion transport within the hierarchical micro-mesoporous network formed by FeCl2 activation.

To explore the charge storage characteristics of the fabricated supercapacitor cell electrochemically, cyclic voltammetry (CV) was conducted. Figure 9 (a) depicts the CV curves of the different potential windows at a scan rate of 10 mV s− 1. At lower potential ranges (0–1 V), the CV curves are almost rectangular in appearance, typical of ideal capacitive behaviour due to the rapid development of the electrical double layer at the electrode-electrolyte interface. As the voltage window is continuously increased to reach 1.5 V, the geometry of the CV profiles does not shift much, also in the form of a rectangle, which suggests the electrochemical stability of the electrode material in this range. Further at high potentials (1.8 V and 2.0 V), it can be noticing small deviations from the ideal rectangular shape can be noticed, possibly due to side reactions and decomposition of the electrolyte. However, the curves still have a quasi-rectangular character, thus indicating that the electrode may be run stably even in the extended potential window, but the most optimal range is 1.0 V. The scan rate dependence in capacitive response has also been assessed by plotting CV characteristics in the optimised potential window at different scan rates. Figure 9 (b) illustrates that the CV curves still assume their rectangular shape even at higher scan rates, which proves the high-rate capability of the electrode material (MKAC). This small distortion and expansion at higher scan rates are characteristic of porous carbon-based electrodes, in which ion diffusion constraints are more pronounced at higher sweep rates. Notably, the fast current response as the scan rate increases shows the fast charge-discharge kinetics and high reversibility of the supercapacitor cell63─66. As the applied potential window is increased, the time of discharge is greatly increased, which confirms the increase in charge storage and better energy density69. sec.p: The long-term electrochemical stability of the MKAC-based symmetric supercapacitor cell was evaluated by performing continuous galvanostatic charge-discharge cycling over 10,000 consecutive cycles, and the results are presented in Fig. 10 (e). The device demonstrates commendable cycling stability, retaining approximately 93–94% of its initial capacitance up to ~ 9000 cycles, followed by a gradual decline to ~ 88% at the end of 10,000 cycles, indicating that the hierarchical microporous architecture of the FeCl₂-activated carbon effectively sustains the electrode integrity under prolonged electrochemical stress48. The Coulombic efficiency (CE), plotted on the right Y-axis, remains consistently close to ~ 99% throughout the majority of the cycling window, with only a marginal decline to approximately ~ 88% observed in the final cycles (beyond ~ 9,500 cycles), which is attributable to minor kinetic irreversibilities and gradual pore blockage at extended cycle numbers a commonly reported phenomenon in microporous carbon-based EDLCs under long-term operation. The inset of Fig. 10 (e) provides a magnified view of the cycling performance. This stable cycling behaviour validates the compatibility of the FeCl₂-activated Murraya koenigii seed-derived carbon electrode with the quasi-solid PVdF-HFP gel electrolyte system, and validates the practical viability of the fabricated device for long-term energy storage applications.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The present work carries significance on multiple scientific and technological fronts. From an environmental standpoint, it successfully valorises Murraya koenigii seeds, an underutilised agricultural residue endemic to the Indian subcontinent, into a high-performance carbon electrode material through a straightforward, single-step FeCl2-assisted carbonisation at 900 °C, effectively diverting bio-waste from landfill within a circular bioeconomy framework. The novelty of this work lies in the dual-functional role of FeCl2 as both a graphitisation catalyst and a micropore-generating agent, yielding an MKAC electrode with a BET surface area of 1605.5 m2 g−1 and 69.5% microporosity, without any external heteroatom doping and in the demonstration of its successful electrochemical integration with a PVdF-HFP quasi-solid polymer gel electrolyte in a separator-free symmetric EDLC architecture, a configuration rarely reported for microporous biomass-derived carbons. In terms of scalability, the single-step synthesis using a low-cost, zero-waste precursor is inherently compatible with industrial-scale carbonisation processes, requiring no exotic reagents or multi-stage processing. Compared to recently reported biomass-derived carbon supercapacitor systems employing conventional liquid electrolytes (Table 4), the MKAC-based quasi-solid device delivers competitive specific capacitance (221.3 F g−1), energy density (15.37 Wh kg−1), and cycling stability (~ 88% retention over 10,000 cycles) while simultaneously offering the practical advantages of leak-proof, flexible, and safe device operation, attributes critical for next-generation portable and wearable energy storage applications.

The practical applicability of the fabricated MKAC-based symmetric quasi-solid-state EDLC is strongly supported by several device-level attributes. The all-solid-state configuration employing the PVdF-HFP polymer gel electrolyte eliminates the fundamental limitations of conventional liquid electrolyte systems, where the device is well-positioned to power low-to-medium consumption portable electronics, wearable health-monitoring sensors, and IoT devices. Furthermore, the low-cost, abundantly available Murraya koenigii seed precursor, combined with the straightforward single-step synthesis, supports scalable and cost-effective manufacturing, a prerequisite for commercial viability within sustainable energy storage frameworks.
